newsitem.title: UK: FUND VIEW - Pictet bullish on ex-communist nations.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Pictet bullish on ex-communist nations.

text.p: Pictet Asset Management has confirmed its bullish outlook for Russia, the former Soviet Union, Eastern Europe and Mongolia with a bid to raise more cash for its London-listed First Russian Frontiers Trust (FRONT).

Pictet, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Pictet & Cie, hopes to raise up to $60 million with a fresh placing and open offer of C shares which will in due course convert to ordinary shares and new warrants. FRONT was launched in November 1994 and its net asset value has risen 39.5 percent to date.

Douglas Polunin, senior investment manager of the $72 million fund, said the investment arena had been transformed since 1992, with rapidly improving settlement and custody facilities, high growth, lower inflation and interest rates.

He believes President Boris Yeltsin's last election victory "effectively removed the systemic risk from the Russian market". "Even if he goes, there are many other candidates to succeed him now," he added.
Other former Soviet republics have no choice but to follow down the reform path, with central and eastern European countries like Poland and the Czech Republic leading the way.
The fund is directly or indirectly invested in the whole region bar Belarus, Moldova, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan, Azerbaijan and Mongolia.
"But the real reason to invest now is the valuations," said Polunin. "It's extremely undervalued."

He cites the Pulp industry emerging world average adjusted capacity value (the market capitalisation of the company divided by the rating capity and adjusted for the balance sheet and condition of plant) as $900/tonne.
The Czech Republic rating is just $300/tonne, with Russia, Poland, the Ukraine and Latvia all under $100/tonne.
The cement sector shows similar undervaluation, with the world average at $140/tonne and Poland at under $80/tonne, and all other countries monitored in the region at under $20/tonne.

The sector analysis also shows how rapidly the new markets become efficient. In the beverage industry, Poland's capacity five years ago was under $10/hl, but now stands at $87/hl, just over the emerging world average of $80/hl.

Polunin admits that these ultra-low valuations are partly a reflection of the stock markets themselves but says that risk factors have been reduced dramatically, with relatively stable currencies and improved company reporting standards.
Pictet picks its investments from a database of over 1,600 companies, sifted for undervalued industrial capacity, cash generative power and capital strength and business franchise.

At the moment the portfolio holds 150 companies in 16 countries, 60 percent of which are in small caps of under $150 million market value. Over 50 percent of the fund is invested in Russia, with a total of 15 percent in Ukraine, Romania, Croatia, Slovenia and Central Asia, where the fund hopes to buy further.
That reduction will be at the expense of already minimal holdings in the Visegrad countries and Baltics.

Breakdown by sector shows an underweighting in financials, which Polunin says are difficult to value, and an overweight in services. The three biggest sectors are Utilities (22.4 percent), Oil and Gas (19.8 percent) and Engineering and Metals (16.8 percent).
Among the major stocks held are Russian steel producer Novolipetsk, bought in February 1995 and held through a battle for control until some profit-taking in March this year.
"It hasn't moved with the market at all," noted Polunin. "Through all the volatility, it just keeping going steadily up."
But he said he was uncomfortable with a narrowing shareholder structure, a factor which also prompted disposal in June of some paper in Bratsk Aluminium, another Russian company.
For the next year Pictet expects that speeded-up privatisations will offer more opportunities and add depth and liquidity to the markets.
